lesson.title: Building the Object a For Loop Actually Talks To
lesson.summary: An iterator implements both __iter__ and __next__, tracking its own position and raising StopIteration when it runs out, which is exactly what the object returned by iter() must do.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter showed a Deck class whose __iter__ method handed off to a list's existing iterator, rather than doing any of the position-tracking work itself. This chapter builds an iterator from scratch: the kind of object that a for loop is actually pulling values from at every step, even when you never see it directly.

An iterator must implement two dunder methods. __next__ returns the next value each time it is called, and raises the built-in StopIteration exception once there is nothing left to return. __iter__, by convention, just returns self, since an iterator is generally expected to also count as iterable (an iterator that could not be handed to a for loop directly would be awkward to use).

```python
class Countdown:
    def __init__(self, start):
        self.current = start

    def __iter__(self):
        return self

    def __next__(self):
        if self.current < 0:
            raise StopIteration
        value = self.current
        self.current -= 1
        return value

for n in Countdown(3):
    print(n)
```

This prints:

3
2
1
0

Trace it the way the for loop does. It calls Countdown(3).__iter__(), which returns the Countdown object itself, since current is 3. Then it calls __next__() repeatedly. The first call sees current is 3, not less than 0, so it saves value = 3, decreases current to 2, and returns 3. The next three calls behave the same way, returning 2, then 1, then 0, and dropping current to 1, 0, and finally -1 along the way. On the fifth call, current is -1, which is less than 0, so __next__ raises StopIteration instead of returning a value. The for loop catches that exception internally and simply stops looping, which is why StopIteration never appears in the printed output even though it is essential to how the loop knows when to end.

This is the real relationship between the iterable protocol and the iterator protocol: they are not two unrelated ideas, the iterator protocol is a stricter version of the iterable protocol. Every iterator is also an iterable (it has a working __iter__, even if that method just returns self), but not every iterable is an iterator (Deck, from the previous chapter, is iterable but has no __next__ of its own, and would raise an AttributeError if you tried to call next() on a Deck object directly). What makes Countdown different from Deck is that Countdown carries its own state, the current attribute, and updates it in place every time __next__ is called, which is exactly the behavior a for loop needs from whatever object it is actually pulling values from at each step.

You can see this machinery directly, without a for loop, by calling iter() and next() yourself.

```python
it = iter(Countdown(1))
print(next(it))
print(next(it))
print(next(it))
```

This prints 1, then 0, then raises StopIteration as an uncaught exception, since nothing here is catching it the way a for loop would. That crash is not a bug, it is the iterator protocol working exactly as designed. A for loop is, underneath, just this same pattern wrapped in something like a try/except that quietly stops on StopIteration instead of letting the program crash.
